lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5 you made a budget. Which comes first: needs, wants or saving? (Needs, then saving, then wants.) Today: a grown-up's monthly budget: pay, bills, saving and fun.
Gross pay is what you earn; net, or take-home, pay is what is left after tax and other deductions. A payslip shows both. A budget plans what the take-home pay will do each month, before it is spent.

Some costs are fixed, the same every month: rent, a phone contract, a bus pass. Others are variable and change: food, electricity, clothes, fun. Fixed costs come first; variable costs are where you can save.
One simple plan is the 50/30/20 rule: about 50% of take-home pay for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for saving. On 2,000 gold, that is 1,000 for needs, 600 for wants and 400 saved.

Pay yourself first: move your saving out on payday, before spending. Build an emergency fund of a few months' needs for surprises. Save for goals: divide the price by the months to find each month's amount.
Track spending for a month: small things add up. A drink of 3 gold every school day is about 60 gold a month. Compare prices, plan meals, and wait a day before buying wants. A spreadsheet can help.

If costs are more than income, the budget does not balance. Fix it early: cut wants, find cheaper deals, or earn more; don't borrow to pay everyday bills. If money worries grow, talk to a trusted adult or a free advice service.
Try it in the world: run My Money Stall in Life for a week of game days. Plan its budget first: stock, saving and a little fun. Did it balance? Next: credit and debt.

exercises.hint: It is what you actually take home to spend.
exercises.explain: Take-home, or net, pay is what is left after tax and other deductions.

exercises.prompt: Pay is 2,000 gold a month. Rent is 800, food 300 and bills 200. How much is left?
exercises.hint: Add up the costs, then take them from the pay.

exercises.prompt: Rent is usually a fixed cost.
exercises.hint: Is it the same every month?
exercises.explain: True: rent stays the same each month.

exercises.prompt: In the 50/30/20 rule, what is the 20% for?
exercises.hint: It is the part kept for later and for surprises.
Could you live safely without it?
exercises.explain: Needs: rent, food shopping, electricity. Wants: cinema trips, a games console, takeaways.

exercises.prompt: Take-home pay is 2,500 gold. Using the 50/30/20 rule, how much goes to wants?
Match each word to its meaning.
exercises.hint: Before or after deductions; steady or changing.
exercises.explain: Gross: before deductions. Net: after. Fixed: the same each month. Variable: it changes.

exercises.prompt: Put a good payday plan in order.
items: spend what is left on fun
exercises.hint: Pay yourself first, then the musts, then the fun.
exercises.explain: Get paid, save first, pay bills, buy needs, then spend what is left.

exercises.prompt: A drink costs 3 gold each school day. How much is that over 20 school days?
exercises.hint: Multiply the cost by the days.

exercises.prompt: An emergency fund is for planned holidays.
exercises.explain: False: it is for surprises, such as a broken boiler or a lost job.

exercises.prompt: Costs are more than income. What is the best first step?
choices: cut wants and look for cheaper deals
exercises.hint: Change what you can control first.
exercises.explain: Cut wants and find cheaper deals; borrowing for everyday bills makes the gap bigger.

exercises.prompt: You want a bike costing 840 gold and can save 70 gold a month. How many months will it take?
exercises.hint: Divide the price by the saving each month.

choices: saving happens before money is spent
exercises.hint: Think what happens to money left until the end of the month.
exercises.explain: Saving first means it really happens, instead of hoping something is left at the end.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: a good budget habit, or a risky one?
items: waiting a day before buying wants
spending all of payday at once
exercises.hint: Does it help the budget balance, or make trouble later?
exercises.explain: Good: tracking, waiting a day, an emergency fund. Risky: borrowing for rent, ignoring bills, spending it all at once.

exercises.prompt: If money worries grow, it helps to talk to a trusted adult or a free advice service.
exercises.hint: Problems are easier to solve early, with help.
exercises.explain: True: free advice services help people plan and solve money problems.
